source_text: Abuti te imperitia faventium tibi, et delitescere sub ambiguitate verborum, quicumque ille fuerit operum nostrorum eruditus lector, intellegit. Reliquum vero vulgus, de quo Propheta loquitur ad Deum: Aestimasti homines sicut pisces maris [n37] ; mutua praegressione decipitur, ac salutiferae discretionis ignarum, totum putat coniungi posse rebus, quod viderit vocibus esse sociatum. Quid vero sit consequens, quid repugnans, quibusque concessis quid lex inexpugnabilis et veneranda orationis cogat inferri, nisi doctissimus attentissimusque non iudicat.
pass_a_gloss: That you abuse the unskillfulness of those favoring you, and hide under an ambiguity of words, whoever that learned reader of our works shall have been understands. But the remaining crowd, of which the Prophet speaks to God: You have estimated human beings as fishes of the sea; is deceived by mutual going-ahead, and, ignorant of a saving discretion, thinks that the whole can be joined to things which it has seen associated in voices. But what is consequent, what is repugnant, and, with which things granted, what the inexpugnable and venerable law of speech forces to be inferred, no one except the most learned and most attentive judges.

lemmas.lexica: LS ratio; Blaise use of reason required for sin

pass_b_english: Any educated reader of our works understands that you abuse your supporters’ ignorance and hide behind ambiguous words. The remaining crowd, of whom the prophet says to God, ‘You have regarded human beings as the fish of the sea’ (Habakkuk 1:14), are deceived as they follow one another’s lead. Ignorant of the distinctions that would save them, they think everything they see joined in words can also be joined in reality. Only a very learned and attentive person can judge what follows, what conflicts, and what the invincible and venerable law of argument requires one to infer from given concessions.

choices.why: For Julian, sin requires rational choice; infants lack usus rationis.
Julian means Scripture's legal/authoritative witness, especially the divine Law as teacher of justice.
rejected: natural law (unless the sentence is philosophical)

anf_compare.notes: Victorian English of some of Julian survives inside NPNF Augustine (chiefly On Marriage and Concupiscence and related anti-Pelagian books). NPNF was not copied. Pass A is a literal gloss of Augustinus.it Latin of Julian's words only; Augustine's replies in the same locus are excluded.

bible_refs.note: From Pass B Scripture tagging; wording follows Julian's Latin, not a modern Bible.

speaker: Julian of Eclanum (words preserved in Augustine, Opus imperfectum contra Iulianum); Augustine's reply at this locus is excluded.
